title: On carrying things quietly for too long
excerpt: We become very good at it. Capable. Dependable. Present for everyone else. And somewhere in there, we forget to wonder whether anyone is present for us.
body:
We become very good at it. Capable. Dependable. Present for everyone else. And somewhere in there, we forget to wonder whether anyone is present for us.

It doesn't happen all at once. It happens in small increments, each one reasonable on its own. You put your needs aside this once because the timing isn't right. And then again, because someone else needs you more. And then again, until the habit of deferring to everything and everyone else is so ingrained that you no longer notice you're doing it.

And then one day something cracks — a conversation that goes wrong, a birthday that passes unremarked, a moment of being overlooked in a way that feels oddly familiar — and you realise you are exhausted in a way that sleep doesn't fix.

That exhaustion has a name. It's the weight of carrying yourself alone, for a very long time.

The women I work with often come to me at this point. Not in crisis, exactly. Just quietly depleted. And almost universally, the first thing they say when they finally start talking — really talking — is some version of: I didn't realise how much I'd been holding.

You don't have to carry it alone. That's not a platitude. It's a practical truth. Some things lighten when they're spoken. Some things clarify when someone else holds the space while you find the words.

That's what I'm here for.
